title: Sort 0s, 1s, 2s in one pass (Dutch National Flag — three pointers).
shortTitle: Sort 0s, 1s, and 2s in One Pass (Dutch National Flag)

s1_definition.profdef: The Dutch National Flag algorithm sorts an array containing only three distinct values, conventionally zero, one, and two, in a single pass using three pointers: a low pointer marking the boundary of the zeros, a high pointer marking the boundary of the twos, and a mid pointer that scans. It partitions the array into three regions, zeros then ones then twos, in linear time with constant extra space, which beats a general comparison sort for this special three-valued case.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India classifies each of the day's transactions on Rajesh's account into three risk buckets: low risk as zero, medium as one, and high as two. The bank wants them physically reordered so all low-risk come first, then medium, then high, in one sweep. Three clerks work the row: one pushes low-risk items to the left end, one pushes high-risk items to the right end, and one walks the middle sorting each item into place. In a single walk the row is grouped perfectly.
s1_definition.oneliner: Low, mid, and high pointers partition the array into zeros, ones, and twos in a single pass.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Dutch National Flag algorithm sorts an array containing only three distinct values, conventionally zero, one, and two, in a single pass using three pointers: a low pointer marking the boundary of the zeros, a high pointer marking the boundary of the twos, and a mid pointer that scans. It partitions the array into three regions, zeros then ones then twos, in linear time with constant extra space, which beats a general comparison sort for this special three-valued case.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India classifies each of the day's transactions on Rajesh's account into three risk buckets: low risk as zero, medium as one, and high as two. The bank wants them physically reordered so all low-risk come first, then medium, then high, in one sweep. Three clerks work the row: one pushes low-risk items to the left end, one pushes high-risk items to the right end, and one walks the middle sorting each item into place. In a single walk the row is grouped perfectly.

**One line to remember:** Low, mid, and high pointers partition the array into zeros, ones, and twos in a single pass.

sections.s2_technical:
You keep three indices. low starts at the beginning and marks where the next zero belongs. high starts at the end and marks where the next two belongs. mid starts at the beginning and scans the array. The invariant is that everything before low is a confirmed zero, everything after high is a confirmed two, and the region from low to mid minus one is confirmed ones; the unknown region is from mid to high.

You loop while mid is less than or equal to high. You look at the value at mid. If it is a zero, you swap the elements at low and mid, then advance both low and mid, because the swapped-in value at mid came from the low region and is already processed. If it is a one, you leave it and just advance mid, because ones belong in the middle. If it is a two, you swap the elements at mid and high, then decrement high only, and crucially you do not advance mid, because the value swapped in from high is unknown and must be examined next.

That last asymmetry is the heart of the algorithm and the most common mistake. When you place a two by swapping with high, the element that comes back to mid has not been seen yet, so you must re-examine it. When you place a zero by swapping with low, the element that comes to mid has already passed through the low region, so it is safe to advance mid.

Because each step either advances mid or decrements high, the unknown region shrinks by one every iteration, so the loop runs linearly and uses only the three index variables, which is constant extra space. It is a single pass, unlike counting then rewriting, which is two passes though also linear.

A senior point is comparing with the counting-sort alternative. Counting the number of zeros, ones, and twos and then overwriting the array is also linear and arguably simpler, and it is often preferred in production for clarity. The Dutch National Flag wins when you must do it in a single pass without a separate write phase, or when the values are not simple integers but objects classified into three groups where you want to move them, not overwrite them. I mention both and pick based on the requirement.

Another senior point is generality: the same three-way partition is exactly the partition step of three-way quicksort, which handles arrays with many duplicate keys efficiently, so understanding this algorithm pays off beyond the toy problem.

A small finance-domain example: `int low = 0, mid = 0, high = n - 1; while (mid <= high) { int v = risk[mid]; if (v == 0) { swap(risk, low++, mid++); } else if (v == 1) { mid++; } else { swap(risk, mid, high--); } }` groups risk buckets in one pass.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India tags each of the day's transactions on Rajesh's account with a risk level of zero for low, one for medium, or two for high, and a review queue must present them grouped so reviewers clear all low-risk quickly, then medium, then focus on high-risk. The grouping must be done in a single in-place pass over a potentially large day, without a separate rewrite phase. The Dutch National Flag three-way partition is exactly this.

This is exactly how the three-pointer sort works in Java — low and high push zeros and twos to the ends while mid scans and classifies.

Problem 2 — Because the review tool reorders the actual transaction records, not just counts, and the day can be very large, the single-pass in-place partition is preferred over counting and rewriting, and the code must get the two-swap non-advance rule right so no transaction is skipped or double-processed. This shows mastery of the subtle pointer rule.

What the code will do: a `RiskSorter` with `sortRiskBuckets(int[] risk)` implementing the three-pointer partition and a private swap helper. The demo groups a mixed day of risk-tagged transactions and logs the grouped result.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the risk tags are `2, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0, 2, 1`.

Step 1: low and mid start at zero, high starts at eight. mid points at a two. We swap positions zero and eight and decrement high to seven; we do not advance mid. The array becomes `1, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0, 2, 2`, and mid still points at the newly arrived value.

Step 2: mid now sees a one at position zero. Ones belong in the middle, so we just advance mid to one. The value stays put.

Step 3: mid at position one sees a zero. We swap positions low zero and mid one, advance both low and mid. The array becomes `0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0, 2, 2`, with low at one and mid at two.

Step 4: mid at two sees a one, so advance mid to three. mid at three sees a two, so we swap positions three and high seven and decrement high to six, not advancing mid. The array becomes `0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0, 2, 2` with the two moved toward the right region.

Step 5: The scan continues, each step either advancing mid or shrinking high, placing zeros via low-swaps and twos via high-swaps, until mid passes high. Every element is examined exactly once in the unknown region, which is why it is a single linear pass.

Step 6: When mid exceeds high the loop ends. The array is now `0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2`, perfectly grouped low then medium then high. The review queue can now present the buckets in order, all achieved in place.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T17:30:00Z INFO Before: [2, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0, 2, 1]
2026-10-26T17:30:00Z INFO Grouped risk buckets: [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2]
2026-10-26T17:30:00Z INFO After (low→med→high): [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [2,0,1,2,1,0,0,2,1]  low=mid=0 high=8
    │
    ▼
  mid scans; partition into 3 regions
    │ 2 → swap(mid,high), high-- (mid stays, value unknown)
    │ 0 → swap(low,mid), low++ mid++ (safe to advance)
    │ 1 → mid++ (belongs in middle)
    │ ... unknown region [mid..high] shrinks each step
    ▼
  [0,0,0 | 1,1,1 | 2,2,2]
    low→    mid→      ←high
    ▼
  Output: grouped low→medium→high in one in-place pass
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Dutch National Flag algorithm sorts an array of only three values in a single pass using three pointers. A low pointer marks where the next zero goes, a high pointer marks where the next two goes, and a mid pointer scans. While mid is at or before high, I look at the value at mid: a zero swaps with low and advances both low and mid, a one just advances mid, and a two swaps with high and decrements high without advancing mid.

The subtle rule that makes it correct is that asymmetry on the two case. When I place a two by swapping with high, the value that comes back to mid has not been examined yet, so I must not advance mid; but when I place a zero by swapping with low, the value that comes to mid has already passed through the low region, so advancing mid is safe. Getting that wrong is the classic bug. Because each step either advances mid or shrinks high, the unknown region shrinks every iteration, so it is linear time and constant space in a single pass.

I compare it with the counting alternative: counting zeros, ones, and twos and then overwriting is also linear and often clearer in production, so I pick the Dutch National Flag when I need a true single pass or when I must move actual objects rather than overwrite integers. I also note it is the same partition used in three-way quicksort, which handles many duplicate keys well.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to group a day's transactions by risk level, zero for low, one for medium, two for high, into a review queue so reviewers clear low-risk fast and focus on high-risk, grouping the real records in place in one pass over a large day. Explaining the three pointers, the non-advance-on-two rule, and the choice versus counting sort shows the interviewer that I understand in-place partitioning deeply, not just as a memorised trick.

keyPoints: Comparison sorts: merge sort O(n log n), quick sort O(n log n) average
Non-comparison: counting sort, radix sort — O(n) for limited range
Kth largest: quickselect O(n) average, heap O(n log k)
